view.stem: Consider two claims about an oblique line and its orthogonal projection onto a plane. (i) Any line perpendicular to the projection is perpendicular to the oblique line. (ii) Any line perpendicular to both the oblique line and its projection lies in the projection plane. Which assessments are correct? Perpendicularity of spatial lines means their directions form a right angle, as in the three-perpendiculars theorem.

options.text: Claim (i) fails: for the plane $z=0$, oblique line through $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,0,0)$, the $z$-axis is perpendicular to the projection but not to the oblique line.
Claim (ii) fails: for the plane $z=0$, oblique line through $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,0,0)$, the line $(0,t,2)$ is perpendicular to both directions but lies outside the plane.
Claim (i) holds for every spatial line perpendicular to the projection, without an additional condition on that line's direction relative to the projection plane.
Claim (ii) forces the perpendicular line itself to lie in the projection plane, rather than allowing a parallel translate outside that plane.

intent.task: Judge both universal statements, separating a direction condition from a positional condition.
intent.source_solution: Independently solving the whole seed: take alpha: z=0, A=(0,0,1), B=(1,0,0), C=(0,0,0). AB has direction (1,0,-1), CB has direction (1,0,0). The z-axis has direction (0,0,1): its dot products with CB and AB are respectively 0 and -1, disproving statement 1. For statement 2 take L={(0,t,2): t real}, direction (0,1,0). Both relevant dot products are zero, but every point of L has z=2. More generally the two perpendicularity conditions make L's direction normal to span(AB,CB), hence parallel to alpha; they do not locate L in alpha. Both original universal statements are false.
intent.unit_reason: One native multiple item compares the two distinct defects in the same purported extension of the theorem. Positive counterexample assertions permit a nonempty true set without inventing a true original statement or using a coded truth combination.
limitations: Selecting supplied counterexamples does not demonstrate producing counterexamples or writing the full refutations independently.

rationales.derivation: The projection direction is (1,0,0), whereas the oblique direction is (1,0,-1). Dotting these with the z-axis direction gives 0 and -1. Thus the premise of (i) holds and its conclusion fails.
The direction (0,1,0) has zero dot product with both (1,0,0) and (1,0,-1). The translate has constant z=2, so it is not contained in z=0.
The line in option a satisfies perpendicularity to the projection but not to the oblique line. The theorem's in-plane direction restriction cannot be dropped.
rationales.misconception: Write AB=AC+CB, set u dot CB=0, then wrongly infer u dot AC=0 because AC is also perpendicular to CB. This replaces an angle relation between two vectors by transitivity of perpendicularity.

rationales.derivation: Perpendicularity fixes a direction, not the height of a parallel translate. The line (0,t,2) satisfies both premises outside the plane.
rationales.misconception: From the direction equation u_z=0, incorrectly impose the point-coordinate equation z=0 on the entire line, discarding its free height intercept.

view.stem: In the three-perpendiculars theorem, replace 'a line in the projection plane' by 'a line parallel to the projection plane'. Is the resulting necessary-and-sufficient condition correct? The oblique line has a nonzero orthogonal projection; perpendicularity compares line directions.

options.text: Yes, in both directions: translating the parallel line into the projection plane preserves each angle involved in the condition.
Only the direction from perpendicularity to the projection to perpendicularity to the oblique line remains valid.
Only the direction from perpendicularity to the oblique line to perpendicularity to the projection remains valid.
Neither direction remains valid when the parallel line is outside the projection plane.

intent.task: Determine whether replacing containment by parallelism preserves both directions of theorem 21.
intent.source_solution: Independently solving the whole seed: a direction u of a line parallel to alpha belongs to alpha's direction space. Translate that line into alpha; its angles with the oblique line and its orthogonal projection do not change. Theorem 21 applies to the translated direction and yields the original equivalence. Equivalently decompose an oblique direction v=p+n with p in alpha and n normal to alpha. Since u dot n=0, u dot v=u dot p; either perpendicularity is exactly the vanishing of the same scalar. A nonzero p is part of being oblique, so no zero-vector perpendicularity is invoked.
intent.unit_reason: The source asks for the validity of one equivalence after one hypothesis replacement. A single assessment of the complete equivalence is the meaningful unit.
limitations: Recognizing the translation argument is not evidence of independently formulating its justification.

The same translation proves the reverse implication as well. The statement incorrectly discards necessity.

rationales.derivation: The same translation proves the forward implication as well. The statement incorrectly discards sufficiency.
rationales.misconception: Use the oblique-line perpendicularity to translate and apply necessity, but wrongly insist the line must meet the projection in order to apply sufficiency.

view.stem: In the figure, $AC\perp\alpha$, $AB$ is oblique, $CB$ is its orthogonal projection, and $m\subset\alpha$ has a nonzero direction vector $\mathbf u=\overrightarrow{MN}$. Use $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AC}+\overrightarrow{CB}$. Which scalar-product reduction establishes $m\perp AB$ if and only if $m\perp CB$?

options.text: $\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{CB}$, because $\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=0$.
$\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}$, because $CB$ is the projection of $AB$.
$\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=0$ for every direction $\mathbf u$ in $\alpha$, because $AC\perp\alpha$.
$(\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{AB})^2=(\mathbf u\cdot\overrightarrow{CB})^2+|\mathbf u|^2|\overrightarrow{AC}|^2$.

intent.task: Identify the decisive scalar-product equality in a proof of both directions of the three-perpendiculars theorem.
intent.source_solution: Independently solving the whole seed before alternatives: the observed arrows run A to C, C to B, and A to B, so AB=AC+CB with these exact orientations. MN is a nonzero in-plane direction of m. Since AC is normal to alpha, MN dot AC=0. Bilinearity gives MN dot AB=MN dot AC+MN dot CB=MN dot CB. AB and CB are nonzero, hence zero dot product characterizes a right angle with m. The same equality proves sufficiency and necessity, not merely one implication. The separated placement of m in the figure confirms the theorem concerns direction angles rather than a required shared intersection.
intent.unit_reason: A decisive proof reduction is a coherent recognition unit. It is not presented as measuring production of an entire written vector proof.
limitations: The learner does not independently write the vector decomposition, invoke bilinearity, or assemble the full two-direction proof.

view.stem: A line $a$ meets the plane $\alpha$. Through a given point $P\in\alpha$, construct a line in $\alpha$ perpendicular to $a$. Perpendicularity is the right angle between spatial line directions. Which construction covers every allowed orientation of $a$?

options.text: If $a\perp\alpha$, every planar line through $P$ works. Otherwise project $a$ orthogonally onto a nonzero planar line $a'$ and draw the unique planar perpendicular to $a'$ through $P$.
In every case, project $a$ onto a planar line $a'$ and draw its unique perpendicular through $P$; the projection is always a nonzero line.
If $a\perp\alpha$, exactly one planar line through $P$ works. Otherwise every planar line through $P$ is perpendicular to $a$.
Let $I=a\cap\alpha$. If $P\ne I$, use $PI$ regardless of its direction. If $P=I$, use any planar line through $I$ regardless of the direction of $a$.

intent.source_solution: Independently solving the whole seed: write a direction of a as v=p+n, with p planar and n normal. Since a meets rather than lies in alpha, n is nonzero. For any planar direction u, u dot v=u dot p. If p is nonzero, a is oblique and there is exactly one planar line through P with u perpendicular to p; this is the line perpendicular to the orthogonal projection a'. If p=0, a is normal to alpha and every planar direction u satisfies u dot v=0, so there are infinitely many solutions through P. The source does not restrict a to being oblique. Under theorem 21's spatial direction convention the requested line need not pass through I=a intersect alpha. Requiring a shared intersection would change the task and, for a general P, could remove existence.

view.stem: From vertex $A$ of rectangle $ABCD$, draw the perpendicular to its plane. Let $M$ be a point on that perpendicular and join $M$ to $B,C,D$, as shown. Determine the right-angle vertices of triangles $MBC$ and $MDC$, and the longest and shortest of $MA,MB,MC,MD$. Which complete result follows without assuming the rectangle is a square?

options.text: $\angle MBC=\angle MDC=90^\circ$; $MC$ is longest and $MA$ is shortest.
$\angle MCB=\angle MCD=90^\circ$; $MC$ is longest and $MA$ is shortest.
$\angle MBC=\angle MDC=90^\circ$; $MB$ is longest and $MD$ is shortest.
$\angle BMC=\angle DMC=90^\circ$; $MA$ is longest and $MC$ is shortest.

intent.task: Recognize the two right triangles and compare all four segments from the point on the normal to the rectangle's vertices.
intent.source_solution: Independently solving the whole seed: take A=(0,0,0), B=(x,0,0), D=(0,y,0), C=(x,y,0), M=(0,0,h), where x,y>0 and h may have either sign. Equivalently their in-plane projections are AB and AD and theorem 21 applies. The squared lengths are MA^2=h^2, MB^2=h^2+x^2, MD^2=h^2+y^2, MC^2=h^2+x^2+y^2. Hence MC is uniquely longest and MA uniquely shortest. MB versus MD depends on x versus y and is not determined. Even if M=A were allowed, these inequalities and the two right triangles remain valid, with MA=0; no unnecessary M-not-A hypothesis is added.

Construct perpendiculars through both $M$ and $N$ to each side of the triangle. Write $F=(MN)\cap(ABC)$, without assuming that $F$ is the triangle's center. For each side line $\ell$, which recipe always constructs the required lines through both points?

options.text: In the triangle's plane draw $FH_\ell\perp\ell$, with $H_\ell\in\ell$. Use the lines $MH_\ell$ and $NH_\ell$.
Let $V_\ell$ be the triangle vertex opposite $\ell$. Use the lines $MV_\ell$ and $NV_\ell$ for every position of $F$.
Choose $T_\ell\ne F$ on the planar line through $F$ parallel to $\ell$. Use $MT_\ell$ and $NT_\ell$.
Through $M$ and $N$ draw lines parallel to $MN$. Use their intersections with $\ell$ as the feet.

The actual rendering has N at the upper endpoint and M at the lower endpoint drawn inside the triangle. The prose says 'through N' but does not itself state which endpoint is the plane foot. Using the named intersection F preserves that wording and gives the same construction without silently relabelling the durable figure or assuming N is the foot. With normal height 60 cm the distance is sqrt(60^2+16^2)=sqrt(3856)=4*sqrt(241) cm. The triangle in part 2 is not right: 20^2+65^2=4625 differs from 75^2=5625. The full seed is solved, but the two independent inputs require different planar-altitude calculations.

view.stem: A point $M$ is equidistant from all vertices of an equilateral triangle of side length $a>0$. Its distance from the triangle's plane is $b\geq0$. Find its common distance to the lines containing the triangle's sides.

options.text: $\displaystyle \sqrt{b^2+\frac{a^2}{12}}$
$\displaystyle \sqrt{b^2+\frac{a^2}{3}}$
$\displaystyle \sqrt{b^2+\frac{a^2}{4}}$
$\displaystyle b+\frac{a\sqrt3}{6}$

intent.task: Use vertex equidistance to identify the projection and compute the point-to-supporting-line distance, not the point-to-vertex distance.
intent.source_solution: Independently solving the whole seed: let O be M's orthogonal projection to the triangle's plane. For every vertex V, MV^2=b^2+OV^2; therefore OA=OB=OC and O is the circumcenter. In an equilateral triangle it is also the incenter. The altitude is a*sqrt(3)/2, and O is one third of that altitude from a side: r=a*sqrt(3)/6, r^2=a^2/12. The perpendicular from O to a side and the normal MO are perpendicular components of the point-to-line perpendicular, giving D=sqrt(b^2+a^2/12) for all three supporting lines. The vertex radius is a/sqrt(3), not the needed side radius. Both signs of the normal height give the same D, and the b=0 case is valid as well.
intent.unit_reason: One common spatial distance captures the projection-center inference and the distinction between the circumradius and inradius. Separate clicks for each identical side would be redundant.
limitations: Recognizing the final formula does not demonstrate constructing the perpendiculars or deriving the center and inradius independently.

rationales.derivation: Equal vertex distances give the equilateral center as the projection. Its side distance is a*sqrt(3)/6, so add a^2/12 to b^2 under the square root.
The term a^2/3 is the squared circumradius, and would calculate distance to a vertex instead of to a side line.
rationales.misconception: Locate the center correctly, then use its vertex radius a/sqrt(3) in place of its side radius a/(2*sqrt(3)).

rationales.derivation: Half the side a/2 is a along-side displacement from a vertex to a midpoint, not the center-to-side perpendicular.
rationales.misconception: Choose the side midpoint as the foot but substitute the half-side length a/2 for the center-to-foot distance.

rationales.derivation: Normal and planar components combine quadratically. For b>0 the sum is larger than the actual distance, so it is not the required formula for all b>=0.

view.stem: Consider these related geometric questions. (R) A point outside a rhombus's plane is equidistant from the lines containing all four sides. Must it be equidistant from all four vertices? (T) A spatial point is equidistant from a triangle's vertices, and also equidistant from the lines containing its sides. What type of triangle is it?. (Q) Answer the same question for a quadrilateral. For (T) and (Q), consider both readings: equality separately within the vertex group and within the side-line group, or the stronger requirement of one common numerical distance to every vertex and every side line. Triangles and quadrilaterals are nondegenerate, with distinct vertices. Select every valid conclusion.

options.text: Under the separate-group reading in (T), the triangle must be equilateral.
Under the separate-group reading in (T), a non-equilateral isosceles triangle can satisfy all the conditions.
Under the separate-group reading in (Q), the quadrilateral must be a square.
Under the separate-group reading in (Q), a rectangle with unequal adjacent sides can satisfy all the conditions.
In (R), equal distances to the side lines do not in general guarantee equal distances to the vertices.
Under the stronger common-numerical-distance reading, neither a nondegenerate triangle nor a nondegenerate quadrilateral can satisfy all the conditions.

intent.task: Classify planar polygons by the two spatial equidistance conditions and distinguish the side-only rhombus hypothesis from the full pair of hypotheses.
intent.source_solution: Independently solving both whole seeds before options. For 340: let O be the orthogonal projection of the outside point M and h>0 its normal distance. Spatial squared distances to side lines are h^2 plus planar squared distances from O. Equality for each pair of opposite parallel rhombus sides forces O onto each strip's midline, hence O is the intersection of the diagonals. Write the rhombus vertices as (+/-p,0) and (0,+/-q). The vertex distances are sqrt(h^2+p^2) and sqrt(h^2+q^2); equality holds exactly when p=q, namely for a square. Thus the original implication is false in general. A concrete full counterexample is vertices (+/-3,0,0),(0,+/-4,0), M=(0,0,12): all side-line distances are sqrt(144+(12/5)^2)=12*sqrt(26)/5, while the two vertex pairs have distances 3*sqrt(17) and 4*sqrt(10), which differ. For 341 under separate-group equality: project the spatial point to O, with normal distance h>=0. Equal vertex distances force all vertices onto a circle centered at O with radius R>0. Equal side-line distances force all corresponding chord lines to have the same unsigned distance r from O. Every side then has length 2*sqrt(R^2-r^2)>0. A triangle is therefore equilateral. A cyclic quadrilateral with four equal nonzero side chords and four distinct vertices is a square: consecutive equal chords have equal unsigned angular steps; changing the sign of a consecutive step would return to the previous vertex, so the four-step cycle uses one orientation and quarter-circle steps. This does not assume the point lies inside the polygon. Conversely the center projection of an equilateral triangle or square, at any normal height, satisfies the separate-group conditions. Under the stronger reading that vertex and side distances share the same numerical value, h^2+R^2=h^2+r^2 forces R=r, making every side chord length zero, impossible for either nondegenerate polygon. The source text of 341(1) ends with '? .' represented in the seed as the question mark followed by a trailing dot without a space. That ink-intent uncertainty is not resolved by an answer lookup, an inferred extra condition, or a lesson edit. The stem preserves the additional dot after its triangle question and explicitly addresses both mathematically distinct equality readings.
intent.unit_reason: The two seeds ask one coherent center-versus-radius classification problem: side-only equality in a rhombus versus simultaneous vertex and side equality in polygons. Combining them prevents the square classification in one question from directly supplying the answer to the rhombus question in another, and avoids separate repeated tests of the same center argument. Native multiple mode tests the distinct consequences and both wording branches without pair-combination codes.
limitations: Selecting the classifications and impossibility result does not demonstrate producing the center/chord proof or inventing a nonsquare-rhombus counterexample.

rationales.derivation: The projection is the circle center by vertex equidistance. Equal distances to the three side lines give equal chord lengths, so all three sides are equal.

A non-equilateral isosceles triangle has a base chord of different length from its two equal side chords. At the circumcenter those chord lines cannot all have the same distance, so the side-line equality fails.
rationales.misconception: Use the triangle's symmetry axis to equate the two equal-side distances, then omit the independent distance condition for the base line, extending the two-side symmetry to all three sides.

rationales.derivation: Equal vertex distances make the quadrilateral cyclic about the projection. Equal chord-line distances make all four sides equal. A four-distinct-vertex equal-chord cycle is a square.

The projection must be the rectangle's center. Its distances to the two pairs of opposite side lines are half the two unequal adjacent side lengths; adding the common squared normal height cannot make them equal.
rationales.misconception: Use the rectangle's equal diagonals to establish vertex equidistance, then mistake equality within each opposite-side pair for equality across all four side lines.

rationales.derivation: A nonsquare rhombus has the same incenter/diagonal-intersection projection forced by its side lines, but unequal half-diagonal lengths. The spatial vertex distances sqrt(h^2+p^2) and sqrt(h^2+q^2) are unequal.
Vertex distance squared is h^2+R^2; side-line distance squared is h^2+r^2. Equality across the two groups forces R=r and zero-length chord sides, contradicting distinct vertices and nondegeneracy.
